nameStory: This moth gets its name from being the 'lesser' or smaller cousin of the larger maple spanworm moth, and its caterpillars are classic 'spanworms' that arch their backs and measure distances by spanning with their bodies like tiny inchworms. The scientific name 'pustularia' refers to small bumps or pustules, likely describing subtle markings on the wings that early scientists noticed under magnification.
description: The Lesser Maple Spanworm Moth is a medium-sized moth in the geometer family, known for their distinctive triangular wing shape when at rest. These moths have subtle, mottled brown and gray patterns that provide excellent camouflage against tree bark. Like all geometers, their caterpillars are the classic 'inchworms' that loop their bodies as they crawl. Adults typically have a wingspan of about an inch to an inch and a half.

idTips.label: Wing Position
idTips.description: Wings held horizontally when resting, creating a distinctive triangular silhouette against bark - quite different from most moths that fold wings roof-like over their bodies

idTips.label: Wing Pattern
idTips.description: Mottled brown and gray coloration with subtle darker lines crossing the wings, feels papery and delicate to touch if handled gently

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Slender body relative to wing size, giving it a more delicate appearance than many stockier moth species

idTips.label: Flight Pattern
idTips.description: Flies with a somewhat weak, fluttering motion rather than the strong, direct flight of sphinx moths or the erratic dance of many smaller moths

idTips.label: Resting Behavior
idTips.description: Often rests head-down on tree trunks during the day, pressed flat against bark with excellent camouflage

habitat: Found throughout New England's deciduous and mixed forests, particularly where maple trees are abundant since the caterpillars feed on maple leaves. Look for adults around porch lights and outdoor lighting in suburban areas adjacent to wooded areas. They're equally at home in lowland forests and hillside woodlands up to moderate elevations.

seasonality.spring: Late spring brings the first emergence of adults in southern New England, typically starting in May. Look for them at night lights as they begin their mating flights.
seasonality.summer: Peak flight season across all of New England from June through August, when adults are most commonly seen. This is the best time to spot them at lights or resting on tree bark during the day.
seasonality.fall: Adult flight season ends by early fall. Eggs overwinter, so no moths are visible during this season.
seasonality.winter: No adult activity - the species overwinters as eggs that will hatch into caterpillars the following spring.

funFact: Despite being called the 'Lesser' Maple Spanworm, this moth has been recorded nearly 4,000 times by citizen scientists in New England alone, making it far more commonly observed than many of its 'greater' relatives - sometimes the little guys win the popularity contest!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other geometer moths, but the horizontal wing position when resting is the key distinguishing feature - remember 'geometers spread like geometry triangles' while most other moths fold their wings like a tent roof over their backs.
contextualKnowledge: The family name 'Geometridae' literally means 'earth measurers' in reference to how their caterpillars appear to measure the earth as they loop along branches, creating the classic inchworm movement that has fascinated children and adults for generations.
compareHints: Compared to its close relative the Red-headed Inchworm Moth, the Lesser Maple Spanworm has more subdued coloration without the distinctive reddish head coloring. Both species rest in the same horizontal wing position, but the Red-headed Inchworm tends to have slightly more contrasting wing patterns and, as the name suggests, often shows warmer reddish-brown tones especially around the head area.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Compared to its close relative the Lesser Maple Spanworm Moth in the same genus, the Red-headed Inchworm Moth has that distinctive reddish-brown head coloring and feeds exclusively on pines rather than maples.
